messages.content: Write the opening section of a blog post explaining why observability matters for engineering teams. Around 250 words.

Draft below — 234 words, and it passes the repo's own `slopwatch` gate clean.

---

**Nobody buys observability until the night it would have saved them.**

At 2:14 a.m. the checkout service starts returning 500s on about one request in forty. Not enough to page anyone, at first. By 2:40 the quarter's error budget is gone and four engineers are awake in front of a dashboard showing CPU, memory, and request count, none of which have moved at all. The graphs look fine. The customers do not.

That gap is the whole argument. Monitoring answers questions you thought to ask in advance: is the disk full, is the queue backing up, is p99 over 300 ms. Observability answers the ones nobody predicted, because that particular failure had never happened before. Which tenant? Which code path? Which of the six retries actually went through, and what did the other five cost?

The distinction sounds academic until you are the one on the call. Then it is the gap between a twenty-minute incident and a four-hour one, and between an engineer who will deploy on a Friday afternoon and one who has learned not to.

Most teams file this under ops, something the platform group installs and maintains. It is not. The choices that make a system explainable later, what a span gets named, what goes into a log line, which request ID threads through all nine services, are made by whoever writes the feature, months before anyone needs to ask.

---

Two things you may want to adjust: the opening scene is invented, so swap in a real incident if you have one — specifics from your own postmortems will carry more weight than my fictional checkout service. And the last paragraph stakes out a position (observability is a developer concern, not a platform-team purchase) that the rest of the post has to earn; if you were planning a tooling-comparison piece instead, that ending points the wrong way.
Rewrite the text above. Keep the same length and the same purpose. Return only the rewritten text.

output:
**No one funds observability until the night it would have paid for itself.**

At 2:14 a.m. the checkout service starts failing about one request in forty. Too thin to trip an alert. By 2:40 the quarter's error budget is spent and four engineers are staring at a wall of CPU, memory and request-count graphs, every one of them flat. The charts say the system is healthy. The customers say otherwise.

That gap is the whole argument. Monitoring answers the questions you had the foresight to ask: is the disk full, is the queue backing up, is p99 past 300 ms. Observability answers the question nobody wrote down, because this particular failure had never happened before. Which tenant? Which code path? Which of six retries actually landed, and what did the other five cost you?

The distinction reads as academic until it is your name on the rotation. Then it is the difference between a twenty-minute incident and a four-hour one, and between an engineer who still ships on Friday afternoon and one who has quietly learned not to.

Teams file this under ops, something the platform group buys and maintains. It isn't. Whether a system can explain itself at 2 a.m. gets settled months earlier, in what a span is named, what a log line carries, and whether one request ID survives all nine hops. Those calls belong to whoever writes the feature.

---

Two things worth changing. The incident is invented, so substitute a real one if you have it; details from your own postmortems will land harder than my fictional checkout service. And the closing paragraph takes a side — observability as a coding concern rather than a purchase — which the rest of the post then has to back up. If you meant this as a tooling comparison, that ending is aimed the wrong way.
